# Agentmux

iOS, iPadOS and Android client for SSH, persistent tmux sessions, and AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Gemini and OpenCode.

Source: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/  |  App Store: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6766158521  |  Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=cc.saxcave.agentmux


---

# Guide — English

## Your AI should be working while you sleep

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-remote-vibe-coding/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

The cost of running agents remotely is standby: the agent waits on you. tmux and SSH move that wait to your phone.

A CLI agent's real cost is standby, not typing: thirty seconds of input, then hours you cannot leave. Run the agent on a machine that stays on, keep its session alive with tmux, and reattach over SSH and Tailscale. Then standby costs a phone and fifteen seconds, and the agent keeps working while you sleep.

You have probably noticed it: the agent does the work, and you are the one tied down. That tie feels like a discipline problem, a question of how well you can step away. It is a physical problem. One terminal window on one laptop has to stay open.

## Where does the time go?

A round of work with a CLI agent almost always has the same rhythm:

```
You talk for 30 seconds → it runs for 5–20 minutes → it needs you to decide something → repeat
```

Lay a whole day out in those proportions and typing is not what eats it. Those 30 seconds are the shortest part. Everything after them is waiting: it reads the project, it edits a dozen files, the test suite runs. Then it stops to ask whether it should handle that migration while it is already in the code. You answer in one line, then wait another five or twenty minutes.

By the end of the day you have produced maybe ten minutes of typing and lost several hours. Those hours were **standby**: you did nothing, and you could not leave, because at any moment it needed one sentence from you.

## The usual setup nails standby to one laptop

That standby has a physical location. The agent runs in a terminal window on your laptop. The window is tied to a shell, and the shell to one machine that has to stay awake. You then have two options, and neither is cheap:

**Sit and wait.** Stay in the chair, watching a screen where nothing happens, so that you can answer within thirty seconds when it asks. An hour of your time buys three replies.

**Or close the laptop.** The process suspends or dies, the session goes, and everything the agent had built up goes with it: which files it read, how far it got, why it chose that approach. Come back later and you open a new window, explain the task from the beginning, and start again.

Either option costs the same, and the cause is **where that machine sits**. The work itself never needed you in the room.

## What three tools undo the tie?

The tie has three layers, and each layer has a standard tool that has been around for decades. Any one of them looks ordinary. Stacked in the right order, they do the whole job:

| Piece | The tie it undoes |
| --- | --- |
| CLI | The agent is a plain-text process that needs no GUI → it can live on another machine |
| tmux | The session is pinned to the server and survives a dropped connection → standby doesn't need you present |
| SSH + Tailscale | Reattach securely from any network, with no public port and no static IP → standby isn't tied to a device or a place |

The order is not arbitrary. The CLI comes first: only then can the agent leave your laptop for the Mac mini at home that never gets switched off. tmux comes next, so the session is pinned to that machine and keeps running after your connection drops. SSH and Tailscale come last, so you can reattach to that same session from the train, the office, or someone else's Wi-Fi, without opening a single outward port on your router.

Drop any one of the three and it falls apart. CLI without tmux: the agent dies when the connection drops. tmux without a secure way in: you can only use it at home.

## Standby costs a phone and fifteen seconds

Once all three are in place, checking in means unlocking your phone for fifteen seconds instead of finding a desk, a seat, and an outlet.

Fifteen seconds changes what the activity is. You stop setting aside a block of time to babysit it. You glance at it in a queue, at a crossing, before bed, reply "use the second approach", and put the phone away. When you look again the agent is still working, and it has moved on without you.

Once standby stops requiring you, the work moves into the hours you were never going to spend at a desk anyway. Hand it a refactor and go to dinner. Start a test-fixing session before bed, and read the results over breakfast. The machine that used to sit idle every night is now the one doing the work.

## What else reaches your agent when you're away?

You have more than one way to reach your own agent from outside. Line the options up against the same criteria and the differences are plain. The last column is the one that matters: it is where people find out they are stuck.

| Approach | Cost of standby | Does context survive | Network setup needed | Can it really edit your files |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Carry the laptop | You need a bag, a seat, and power | Stops when you close the lid | None, but the machine has to travel with you | Yes, the files are local |
| VNC remote desktop | Needs a big enough screen, and a desktop UI driven by a finger | Survives as long as the desktop session does | Punch through for VNC, or stand up a VPN | Yes |
| Browser-based agent | Low: just open a browser | Lives on someone else's server | None | It edits a copy in a cloud sandbox, not the one on your machine |
| Cloud environments like Codespaces | Low, but you need a browser | The container gets reclaimed after enough idle time | None, but the project goes to the cloud and you're billed by usage | Yes, but it's the repo inside the cloud container |
| General SSH app | A phone is enough | Holds up, thanks to tmux | Securing the way in is on you | Yes, but the interface is a desktop terminal ported across as-is |
| Agentmux | A phone, fifteen seconds to reattach | tmux is on the server, regardless of the phone | Tailscale, with no public port | Yes, the copy on your own machine |

An agent in someone else's cloud sandbox edits a copy, always. Your `.env` is not in that sandbox. Neither is the internal package you installed this morning, or the database that only runs locally. Take the SSH and tmux road and the agent sits on your machine, in your environment, editing your files. The only thing that changed is that your phone is watching it.

Not sure where to start? Help me pick a track.

## Why not Cursor or VS Code

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-not-gui-ide/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

On a desktop the IDE agent usually wins. On a phone a terminal wins: a byte stream can be stored and reattached.

An agent inside Cursor or VS Code runs as part of a GUI process, so it needs a screen, a logged-in desktop, and someone sitting in front of it. A CLI agent's interface is a stream of characters, which tmux can store whole and reattach on any device. The difference is architectural, not a matter of taste.

You already have Cursor, or VS Code with an agent extension, and it works well. Learning SSH and tmux for the same job pays off in one situation: you are not sitting at the machine.

## The difference is architectural, not a preference

An agent inside a GUI IDE is part of that GUI program. It lives in the application's process, its state sits in that window's memory, and its output is painted onto a canvas. That is why it needs a screen, a logged-in desktop session, and a person in front of it. Close the window and the agent ends with it. Nobody overlooked anything: the agent grew out of that process.

A CLI agent's interface is a byte stream: characters in, characters out, and nothing graphical anywhere along the way. A stream like that can be **attached to, detached from, and attached again**. tmux does the bookkeeping, because an 80×24 matrix of characters can be stored whole and redrawn onto any screen: your laptop, your phone, a friend's iPad. Changing devices loses nothing, because what changed hands was only ever characters.

That is the whole reason a CLI agent works remotely: **a canvas of pixels cannot be serialised and reattached, and a matrix of characters can**. It is a claim about capability, not about who prefers keyboards.

## What happens when you close the laptop mid-task?

Suppose you hand the agent a large refactor at the end of the working day. It needs twenty minutes at least, and you are leaving now.

| Cursor left open | tmux + Claude Code |
| --- | --- |
| Close the laptop | Agent stops | Agent keeps running |
| Two hours later | Open it, context is gone, start again | Open your phone, it's finished |

Nothing in the right-hand column depends on how clever the agent is. That session never lived on your laptop. It lives on the machine that was never switched off, and your laptop was attached to it for a while. Closing the lid ended the connection, and the work carried on without you.

Cursor has cloud background agents now, and those do keep running after you close the laptop. What keeps running is a copy inside Cursor's own remote sandbox, not the agent on your machine, which puts them with the browser agents and Codespaces discussed elsewhere on this site. The left-hand column still describes what happens to the agent on your machine.

## "Couldn't you just use remote desktop?"

This is the most common objection, and in theory it is airtight. The desktop is still running on that machine. VNC back into it and Cursor is still open, so the problem looks solved.

In practice the two ship different things. **VNC sends pixels. SSH sends characters.** One full screen update is hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes of image data, and the same screen as characters is a few kilobytes of text, a gap of roughly three orders of magnitude.

You hit that gap on ordinary days. On a train, in a lift, anywhere you are down to one bar, VNC turns into a slideshow and a single scroll takes three seconds to redraw. SSH characters arrive instantly on the same connection.

Even with bandwidth to spare you are still facing a desktop UI built for a mouse and a 1440p display, crammed onto a six-inch touchscreen. Hitting a menu item means zoom, aim, tap. An interface nobody designed for touch does not get easier just because the connection is fast.

## At your desk the IDE is often the better tool

An IDE is not the wrong tool, and at your desk it is often the better one: go-to-definition, refactoring, a debugger, none of which work over a phone connection. **An IDE suits "you are here and you are driving". A CLI agent plus remote access suits "it is running and you are checking in".** Use both if you can: the IDE on the Mac while you are at the desk, and Agentmux to rejoin the same agent on the same project once you have left it.

Agentmux is not trying to replace your IDE. It replaces the part where you sit in a chair and wait. Then you put the phone in your pocket, the signal drops in the tunnel, and what happens to that session is a problem of its own.

## Why the strongest coding agents live in the terminal

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-cli/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Why coding agents live in a terminal: full filesystem access and permission to execute. What a shell is, and when a GUI tool wins.

A CLI agent is a coding agent you talk to in text. It runs in a terminal on a machine you own, a Mac, a Linux box, or a server. There it inherits your permissions: read every file in the project, run any command, read the result back. Agents live in terminals because no other interface grants all three.

"CLI" still reads like a punishment: no mouse, no buttons, one blinking cursor. Yet Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and OpenCode all live there. Their makers are not purists. The terminal grants two things no other interface grants together: full access to your files, and permission to run commands. That same permission is why it asks you before running anything.

## What is a terminal, once you strip the buttons away?

Two programs are stacked here, and beginners blame the wrong one. The **terminal** is the display layer: it draws a grid of characters and forwards your keystrokes. Behind it sits the **shell** (zsh, bash, fish), which waits for a line of text, runs it, and prints what that program wrote.

That thinness is why an agent can drive a real project end to end. The commands it types are commands you would have typed, and the errors it reads are the errors you would have seen.

## Three things you read off a terminal screen

Three parts of that screen carry the meaning. The rest is decoration.

```
yuki@mini ~/projects/auth (main)
$ npm test

 ✓ src/session/refresh.test.ts  (6 tests)
 ✗ src/session/expire.test.ts > drops a session after expiry

     Tests  1 failed | 41 passed (42)

$ echo $?
1
```

**The prompt** is that first line. It says who you are, which machine you are on, which directory, and which branch. That line stops being decoration once the machine is not in front of you. After an SSH login it is how you tell your laptop apart from a server you forgot you were still logged into.

**Standard output** (*stdout*) is the text the program wrote. The second stream, *stderr*, keeps its complaints separate so the real output stays readable.

**The exit status.** Every command leaves one integer behind, and the shell hands it to you as `$?`. Zero means the program claims success. An agent reads that number rather than the words "1 failed", and a `1` is its signal that the loop is not closed yet.

## The interface decides what an agent can reach

A browser agent cannot see a single file on your computer. It lives inside a tab. An IDE plugin sees the files you have open but usually stops at suggestions: it cannot touch git, cannot run your tests, and cannot install packages.

A CLI agent holds the permissions you hold. It reads the whole repo, runs `git commit`, runs the test suite, and installs dependencies. Access arrives in three tiers, and the risk climbs with each one:

- **Read.** Every file in your home directory, including the keys in `.ssh`.

- **Write.** Inside a git project, a bad edit is one `git checkout` away. Outside one, nothing rolls it back for you.

- **Execute.** Anything you could type, including a migration, a force-push, or an `rm -rf` pointed at the wrong path.

No vendor designed this gap to please anyone. It is the permission set that comes with the terminal, and every other interface gives away less of it.

## Which commands can it run that a sandboxed agent cannot?

"Execution rights" is an abstraction. Here is the same thing as lines on a screen:

```
npm test
npx vitest run src/session/expire.test.ts

git status --short
git commit -m "fix: expire sessions on the dot"

npm install date-fns@3
npm run build

psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f db/schema.sql
curl -sf localhost:8000/health | jq .db
```

A hosted sandbox has nowhere to run those. That `psql` connects to a database that exists only on your machine, using a URL from a `.env` file that was never uploaded. That `npm install` pulls an internal package from a private registry named in your `.npmrc`. Those `git` commands run in a clone that carries your remote, your hooks, and your signing key.

A sandboxed agent can hand you a patch, but it cannot observe what that patch did. An agent that cannot see the result of its own edit cannot finish the task.

## The loop that closes without you pressing anything

You send one line: "fix this bug." A dozen commands of that kind follow, and your hands stay off the keyboard:

- It greps for the failing message, reads three files, edits one.

- It runs `npm test`, reads the exit status, sees `1`.

- It narrows to one case, edits again, reruns the whole suite, gets `0`.

- It commits, applies the migration locally, and curls the endpoint that was broken.

Not one step in that chain needs a click. Put the same agent in a browser tab or an IDE plugin and it stalls at step two. It can produce the edit, but it cannot run the suite, so it waits for you to run the tests and tell it what happened. You have become the test runner. That is a permissions problem, not a model-quality one.

## Why is a byte stream worth more than a window?

The program does not live inside the terminal window. It is attached to a **pseudo-terminal**, a kernel object with two ends. Bytes go in one end and come out the other, and your window is whoever happens to be holding the far end right now. Three things follow from that.

- **It can be saved.** `npm test > build.log` writes that text to a file, which another program can read a year later. A GUI's canvas is a picture, and a picture is not a record.

- **It can be chained.** `git ls-files | grep .env` feeds one program's output into the next program's input.

- **It can be moved.** Nothing in the definition says the two ends have to be in the same place. tmux parks the session on the server, and your screen attaches, detaches, and attaches again from another device.

The third one is the point of this guide. **A byte stream can be redirected, stored, replayed, and reattached from somewhere else. A rendered window cannot.** Persistent sessions, SSH, and the same agent on your phone all follow from that one property.

## What does full access cost you?

The permission that lets an agent migrate your database is the permission that lets it delete one. That is why an agent stops mid-task and asks: "Run this command?" The prompt is not timidity. An agent that ran everything without asking would be deciding about your `.ssh` directory and your production database on your behalf, from guesswork. The prompt is where you draw the line between tier two and tier three, and it can only be drawn at that moment: the command is known, and it has not run yet.

Two habits cover most of the risk. **Read the command, not the summary:** "I'll clean up the build cache" is a description, and only the line under it has consequences. **Approve a category once:** if it asks you to run tests forty times a day, write one rule that lets `npm test` through.

A prompt you were going to approve anyway costs ten seconds. One you approve by mistake, against a live database, costs a day and a restore. That ratio is why AI Permission Review exists: a blacklist blocks what is obviously dangerous, an allowlist passes what you already trust, and a model judges the rest.

## When a GUI is the better tool

A terminal is not the right interface for everything you do to code. These are strictly worse in text:

- **A live debugger.** Set a breakpoint, step through the loop, inspect a variable at frame four.

- **Anything visual.** Layout, spacing, a colour that is almost right. Asking an agent to describe a screenshot is worse than looking at one.

- **Reading a large diff.** Two thousand lines side by side is why you review an agent's work in a GUI, even when the agent wrote it.

- **Still learning.** An editor underlines the exact token where you went wrong, which teaches faster than a wall of stack trace.

The line here is not skill against laziness. It is **"you are here and driving"** against **"it is running and you are checking in"**. At a desk an IDE is often the better instrument, and the people who get the most out of a CLI agent keep both. That division of labour is its own article.

The terminal puts an agent on your machine, and its output is characters that can live anywhere. So that machine does not have to be the one you are sitting at. Getting there from somewhere else is SSH's job.

## SSH is a tunnel to a machine you own

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-ssh/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

SSH is an encrypted channel to another computer: host, user and port, why keys beat passwords, and why no port faces the internet.

SSH is an encrypted channel between your device and another computer. You send keystrokes, that machine runs the commands, its output comes back, and no hop in between can read any of it. To run a coding agent remotely, SSH is how your phone reaches the machine the agent runs on.

The last article argued that an agent does its best work in a terminal, with full access to a filesystem and permission to execute. That terminal does not have to be in your pocket. It can be the Mac mini at home that never gets switched off, or the workstation at the office, as long as your phone can route to it.

## Why another machine instead of a cloud service?

Browser agents and cloud IDEs connect you to a machine too. The difference is whose machine it is.

SSH connects you to your own. Your files and API keys are already there, along with every package you installed and every environment variable you set. Nothing has to move onto someone else's server, and the changes stay where you made them, so there is nothing to sync back afterwards.

The trade-off runs the other way too. A cloud environment is the better answer if you own no machine that stays on, or if a whole team needs one identical starting point. Your machine has to be awake, reachable, and set up by you.

## What you actually type: host, user, port

Every SSH connection needs three things, and the command writes them on one line:

```
ssh -p 22 sax@mac-mini
```

| Part | What it names |
| --- | --- |
| Host | Which machine: a name such as mac-mini, or an address such as 100.101.102.103 |
| User | Which account on it. You get its files, permissions, and shell, and nothing above that account |
| Port | Which door. SSH's default is 22, so the field usually goes empty |

Two of those three are where beginners get stuck. The host has to be an address your phone can route to; the next section covers which ones. And the user has to exist on that machine: an agent runs as that user, and it can touch exactly what that user can.

## Why not your LAN address or your public IP?

The first address you find is in your network settings: something like `192.168.1.23`. Try it from a laptop on the same Wi-Fi; that is what it is for. It is a private address handed out by your router, valid only inside your own network. A phone on mobile data has no route to it.

The second is the public address your home connection shows the internet, with a port forwarded through the router to that one machine. That road works, and it is the one to avoid. Scanning bots try logins against every address in the world, around the clock, and an exposed port starts collecting attempts within a day. One mistake in the router settings opens the whole network instead of one machine.

Use a third kind: a private address only your own devices can see. Tailscale gives each machine a MagicDNS name or a `100.x` address, and nothing else on the internet knows those exist. That goes in the host field, at home and away.

## Keys are safer and need less typing

SSH takes passwords or keys, and the choice gets framed as security versus convenience. Keys are better at both.

A key pair is two small text files. The private one stays on the device that connects. The public one is computed from it and copied onto the machine you want to reach, into `authorized_keys` inside that account's `~/.ssh` directory. The arithmetic runs one way. The public half comes from the private half, and you cannot recover the private half from the public one. `ssh-keygen` makes a pair in seconds.

At login the two halves prove the match and you type nothing. A password has to survive repeated guessing, and a key is long enough that guessing never pays. Set it up once and every connection afterwards works the same way.

Put a passphrase on the private key, because a key is a file. Copy it off an unlocked laptop and someone else holds your key. The passphrase makes that copy worthless by itself, and unlike a login password it never crosses the network: it unlocks the key on the device, and what travels is a signed answer to a challenge.

On a phone the difference matters more. A typed password goes over the wire on every connection, handing anyone who can reach the port a fresh guess. A key answers a challenge instead, and the private half never leaves the device. If the key is in place and still refused, the usual causes are few: wrong path, wrong user, wrong permissions.

## Where does the app keep my key?

Agentmux collects no personal data. Usage statistics are anonymous and optional; turning them off changes nothing about how it connects. Passwords, keys, and passphrases go into the operating system's hardware-backed credential storage. Your SSH traffic is never logged: the channel is encrypted between your device and your machine, and the app is not a relay.

## Why the fingerprint prompt appears the first time

The first time you reach a machine, before any password or key, the client prints a line about the host's authenticity, a short string of hex, and a yes or no. That string is the server's fingerprint: a readable summary of the host key the machine signs with. Nothing has gone wrong. SSH is authenticating the other direction.

A password or key proves you to the machine. A host key proves the machine to you. Without that second half, anyone between your phone and your Mac mini could answer in its place and read what you send. On a first connection there is no stored copy to compare against, so the client asks you to accept it and remembers it from then on.

It earns its keep later. Reconnect to a machine whose fingerprint has changed and the client refuses. Either you reinstalled the system, or something else is answering.

## Do you have to turn your computer into a server?

People hear "SSH" and picture racks in a data centre. You are flipping a switch. On a Mac it is System Settings → General → Sharing → Remote Login. On Linux it is usually starting a service called `sshd`, which most distributions already ship.

Nothing else about the machine changes. It is still your everyday computer, with one more door you can knock on from outside. If you would rather not remember the order of operations, the setup page asks three questions and hands back a checklist.

## SSH is not a VPN or a remote desktop

Three things SSH does not do:

| Not this | What that would mean | What SSH does instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A VPN | Everything your phone sends routed into your home network | One channel to one port on one machine. Nothing else becomes reachable |
| A mounted filesystem | Your remote disk appears as a folder | Bytes on request. A file browser fetches and pushes each file itself |
| Screen sharing | Pictures of a desktop, steered with a finger | Text both ways: keystrokes out, printed output back |

That last row is a real limit, not a flaw in this tool. Software that exists only as a window you click cannot be driven over SSH, which is the same boundary the previous article drew: an agent that speaks text is an agent that fits down the tunnel.

Then you put your phone away, the tunnel drops, and the agent dies with it. Unless the session was never living inside your connection: that is what tmux is for.

## Keep the agent running after you put your phone away

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-tmux/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

tmux is a terminal multiplexer: the session lives on the server, so a dropped SSH detaches instead of killing the agent.

tmux is a terminal multiplexer: it keeps a terminal session running on the machine you connect to, rather than inside the connection you came through. For an AI coding agent, that is the difference between surviving and dying. SSH connections drop when a phone locks or a signal goes, and a dropped SSH normally kills the agent's shell.

You put your phone away, the SSH tunnel drops, and the agent dies with it. That is mechanics, not bad luck.

When the connection goes, the kernel closes the pseudo-terminal your login was using. It sends **SIGHUP** (hangup) to every process attached to it: your shell, and the agent inside it. A process that does not catch that signal on purpose terminates by default, and the kernel throws away whatever was half-finished. SSH was only the path the connection came along. It was never what kept the agent alive.

## tmux lets the session live somewhere else

tmux opens a session on the server, and your agent runs inside that session rather than inside the SSH connection that keeps dropping.

The mechanism is a process. The first time you type `tmux`, it starts a background program called the tmux *server*, which stays alive under your user account. Sessions belong to that process, and each one gets its pseudo-terminal from it instead of from `sshd`.

When the connection goes, `sshd` closes its own pseudo-terminal, and only your tmux client is attached to it. The client exits. The session keeps running.

## What is a session, a window, a pane?

People use three nouns for three different things, and only the first one keeps your agent alive.

| Word | What it is | What it means for an agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| session | A named place to work on that machine, holding its own processes | The thing that survives. Name it once |
| window | A tab inside a session; most people give each agent one | Switch away and it keeps running |
| pane | A split inside a window: agent left, tests right | Two things visible on a phone screen |

A fourth word: a **client** is the terminal looking at a session. A session with zero clients is normal. It is detached, still running, and nobody is watching it.

Names matter. The session you made with `tmux new -s work` is still findable a week later, while an unnamed session is just a number you have to look up.

## Is detaching like turning off a television?

Switch a TV off and the picture in your living room is gone. The broadcast never stopped. Turn it back on and you are on the same channel, wherever it has got to by now.

tmux calls those two actions **detach** and **attach**: close the window, open it again. Neither one touches what is running on the machine.

The analogy hides one thing, and it works in your favour. A television learns nothing while it sits switched off, but a tmux session keeps its output. Attach an hour later and you can read the hour you missed by scrolling back through it.

## Which commands do I type?

Start with four:

```
tmux new -s work          # make a session named work
claude                    # start the agent inside it
tmux ls                   # list sessions: work: 1 windows
tmux attach -t work       # look at it again, from anywhere
```

**Detach is a key press, not a command.** Press Ctrl-b, let go, then press d. That first key is the *prefix*: tmux takes it, and the next key says what to do. Two more are worth learning:

- `Ctrl-b d` detaches. The terminal becomes an ordinary shell again, and the session keeps running.

- `Ctrl-b c` makes a new window; `Ctrl-b %` splits a window into panes.

If the machine answers `tmux: command not found`, the fix is on the troubleshooting page.

## A dropped connection does not interrupt the agent

You lose signal on the train, again in a lift, again when you switch Wi-Fi. Attach to the same tmux session every time and you can drop ten times without interrupting the agent once. It never notices, because it was never living inside your connection.

The three cases people worry about on a phone are one event described three ways:

- **The phone locks.** The system suspends the app, the connection comes apart, and nothing reaches the agent. It keeps working.

- **No signal for twenty minutes.** The connection dies quietly and the tmux client dies with it. The session stays detached and untouched.

- **You kill the app or swipe it away.** A process on the phone is gone, and the session was never inside it. Close a laptop's terminal window and tmux behaves the same way.

Detach does not pause anything. While you are gone the agent keeps reading files, editing them, and spending your quota. That is the point of it, and it is why you answer a prompt that is waiting before you walk off.

## Can two devices watch the same session?

Yes, and there is no trick to it. Several clients can attach to one session at the same time. Start the job from your phone in a queue, attach from your laptop at work, and you are looking at the same screen mid-sentence rather than a copy of it.

Keys from either device go to the same program, so only one person types at a time. Attaching moves nothing: the session stays on the machine that made it, which is why your phone and your laptop agree. A session you started by hand in a laptop terminal is there for the app too.

## How the app handles these sessions

Agentmux is built on the same split. A disconnect on the phone's side is a detach and nothing more: reconnect and you are back at that session, further along. Type the commands above in its terminal and it is still the same session.

The app takes two chores off your hands. If the machine has no tmux, the app installs it, working out whether your machine uses apt, yum, dnf, pacman, apk, or brew. If an agent sits where the shell can't see it, the app probes that PATH problem. Persistent sessions are in the free single-server tier, so nothing here is paid. The setup page turns it into a checklist.

## What tmux does not do

tmux answers one question, whether a process outlives your connection, and leaves the rest alone.

- **A reboot of the server ends every session.** They live in the tmux server's memory, so a power cut or an unattended upgrade ends the agent with them. What survives is what reached the disk: files changed, commits made, the branch you were left on. Git is the save file, not tmux.

- **It does not undo a command the agent already ran.** tmux keeps the output of that command, but it does not roll the files back.

- **`tmux kill-session -t work` really does kill it.** So does quitting the last window, or the agent crashing. `tmux kill-server` takes every session with it, and tmux does not ask first.

- **It does not keep the machine awake.** A Mac mini that stays on is a different case from a laptop that sleeps when you shut the lid, and a machine that powers off loses the session.

Checking this takes two minutes. SSH in, run `tmux new -s work`, start an agent, press Ctrl-b then d, close the connection, and run `tmux attach -t work`. The same screen comes back, further along, with one question waiting for you.

So the agent survives you putting the phone away. One problem left: getting in from outside without opening a port to the whole internet. Tailscale answers that.

## Tailscale: no port open to the internet

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/what-is-tailscale/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Tailscale builds a WireGuard mesh between your own devices, so your phone connects to a MagicDNS name or a 100.x address and no port opens.

Install Tailscale on your computer and on your phone, sign both in to the same account, then connect with SSH to the machine's MagicDNS name or its `100.x` address. Tailscale builds an encrypted WireGuard mesh between your own devices, so you open no port on your router to the internet and never point SSH at a public address.

The agent survives a dropped connection, which only helps if there is somewhere safe to reconnect from. The obvious answer is to expose port 22 to the internet, and that is the fastest way into trouble. Scanning bots knock on port 22 across every IP on earth, around the clock.

A second problem is duller and harder to dodge. Your home IP is dynamic, and the machine sits behind NAT, sharing one outward address with everything else at home. There was never a public address there to open.

## Three jobs on the router, all by hand

The traditional fix meant the router itself: port forwarding so a public port reaches the machine, a DDNS service binding a hostname to today's IP or a static IP from your ISP, then firewall rules kept straight by hand.

Get one step wrong and you cannot get in, or you have exposed your whole home network. Get them all right and a door still faces the internet.

## Why does port forwarding plus a dynamic IP keep breaking?

Four parts have to hold at the same time, and any one of them gives way at an inconvenient moment.

- **The address changes.** Your ISP reassigns it, and a DDNS client needs a few minutes to catch up. For a window after every change, nothing you saved points at home. If that update fails while you are away, the hostname belongs to somebody else.

- **Sometimes the address is not yours.** Behind carrier-grade NAT your router holds an address inside the ISP's own network, so no forward can work.

- **One forward is one more door** into a network shared with a smart TV and an old camera.

- **It has to stay right forever.** A firmware update resets the rules; a new router means rebuilding them.

The worst part is the debugging. You are on mobile data, trying to fix a home router from your phone, and the machine you want is unreachable.

## What Tailscale does

Tailscale is a WireGuard mesh. Install it on each device, sign in to the same account, and the devices build an encrypted link straight between themselves. The setup opens no public entry point and leaves no port on the internet for a bot to scan.

Each device makes a WireGuard key pair, and the private half never leaves the device. The public halves are exchanged, and the tunnels are built from them. The account is bookkeeping: it introduces devices, tracks where each is reachable, and hands out private addresses the public internet does not route to.

MagicDNS gives each device a name you can remember and resolves it for you, so NAT, an address that changed overnight, and the switch from home Wi-Fi to mobile data all stay out of sight.

## Why the mesh works when your phone has no address

Mobile data makes it worse. Your phone has no public address either: on 4G and 5G it sits behind carrier-grade NAT, sharing one outward address with many other subscribers. A design that depends on incoming connections fails at both ends.

A mesh works the other way round: both sides only have to send packets *outward*. The phone sends one, the machine sends one, each learns where the other appears to be, and the two attempt a direct path through their NATs. WireGuard supplies the encryption, and the mesh supplies the introductions. Where no direct path exists, traffic falls back to a relay and stays encrypted end to end.

## A private address only your devices can reach

Your machine gains a private address. Only devices signed in to the same Tailscale account can see it or reach it. The scanning bots do not know it exists, because it never appeared on the public internet.

From here on, SSH goes to that address instead of a port 22 that gets knocked on all day.

## Which address do you type?

The LAN address is the one to skip. Your machine holds three addresses at once, and only two of them are worth saving.

| Address | Where it works | Use it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LAN, e.g. 192.168.1.23 | That Wi-Fi only | No. On mobile data it routes nowhere useful |
| The ISP's address for the router | Nothing under carrier-grade NAT | No. It changes, and it is the router's |
| MagicDNS name, e.g. mac-mini.tail1234.ts.net | Any network, tunnel up at both ends | Yes. Save this one |
| 100.x.y.z | Same as the name | Yes, when name resolution is the broken part |

A LAN address identifies a local network, not your machine. Save the name, and the entry survives the machine changing Wi-Fi, changing IP, or moving flats. `tailscale status` prints both.

When SSH fails although both devices look connected, check the address first. Tailscale says connected, SSH still can't reach it covers that, including a signed-out machine.

## What does the mesh cost you?

There are three costs, and you should know them before you are on a train.

**One more program on the machine.** It starts at boot, updates itself occasionally, and has its own bugs. That is one more thing to rule out before you blame SSH.

**A control plane you need at the wrong moment.** Traffic goes device to device, but the introductions do not. A new laptop, a replaced phone, or stale credentials are not on your network until they sign in. Fail that sign-in while you are out and the machine is fine but unreachable. Keep another way in.

**A phone that has to stay connected.** The tunnel is a VPN profile, and phones drop those: after a restart, when another VPN takes over, or when you dismiss the prompt. Check it before debugging anything else. It carries only traffic to your own addresses.

## A private network still needs a key

A machine nobody can reach from the internet still needs a lock on the door, for two reasons.

The mesh's security is now your account's security: any device that signs in is inside, and inside means a device you already trusted. A laptop left in a taxi is inside the network you built, where every machine is reachable and nothing else checks it. A key means the machine still has to prove something.

The second reason is defence in depth. The mesh keeps strangers out; a key stops a stranger who is already inside from going further. Two independent things have to fail before anyone reaches your project. A password is one guessable thing, and a key is not. How keys do the proving covers the mechanics.

## When you don't need Tailscale

If the machine and the phone are on the same Wi-Fi and always will be, skip this. The LAN address works, you install nothing, and you sign in to nothing. You lose it the moment you walk outside.

A hosted server changes the arithmetic. Its address does not move, there is no router of yours to configure, and a failed experiment cannot lock you out. The risk moves to port 22 facing the internet permanently. Some people still run the mesh there, to put SSH behind a private address; others keep it public and lean on keys. What is not workable: a password on an exposed port.

If you already reach the machine through a network someone else runs, a work VPN for example, take that path. Two overlapping tunnels make debugging worse without making the connection better. If you are not sure which case you are in, the setup page asks three questions and hands you a checklist.

The way in is settled. What is left is the phone in your hand, and what that phone assumes about why you are there.

## Why not Termius or Blink

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/why-agentmux/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Agentmux vs Termius and Blink: five capability differences, and the cases where Termius is the better tool.

A general SSH client assumes you opened it to type commands. Agentmux assumes you opened it to rejoin an agent that is already running. Take Termius or Blink if you need Mosh, SOCKS5 forwarding, or host sync across platforms. Take Agentmux if your work is coding agents on several servers rather than one-off commands on one host.

Both apps speak SSH and both hand you a prompt. What separates them is how much thought went into reattaching, and every row below follows from that. The five capabilities described here are all checked against the current source.

## Two tools built on different assumptions

A general SSH client is built around a host and a shell: it hands you a working prompt, then stays out of the way. What happens after that prompt is yours.

Agentmux is built around an agent that is already running somewhere. Its job is to shorten the distance from your pocket to that process. Three consequences follow, and the last two are where a good general client stops being a substitute. That is not a build-quality problem: those behaviours were never its product.

- **What you see first.** A host, or the sessions running on it.

- **What a dropped connection costs.** A prompt you re-navigate, or the screen you left.

- **What the app does while you are away.** Nothing, or a Lock Screen progress line and a sound at the end.

## What each one does, capability by capability

One row per capability. Where you cannot check a competitor's behaviour from outside its app, the cell says so.

| Capability | General SSH client | Agentmux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Back to a tmux session | tmux ls, then tmux attach -t | Sessions listed on connect; one tap reattaches |
| After a drop | The prompt returns; finding the session is on you | A detach, not a death: you land on the screen you left |
| A twenty-minute agent run | No notion of a run to report from | Dynamic Island and Lock Screen progress; a sound at the end |
| Prompt to allow a command | You are the reviewer, in the chair | AI Permission Review: blacklist, allowlist, AI judgement; suggests or presses the key (Pro) |
| One line in a file | Vim over SSH, on a phone keyboard | Runestone editor, Ink Markdown preview, branch tools, Files app (Pro) |
| Private keys | Not verifiable from outside | Keychain / Keystore, never the local database; iCloud sync carries server names only |
| Automation from outside | Nothing to call: no session or agent model exposed | 6 App Intents over four entity types: Server, Project, TMUXSession, RecentSession |
| Unreliable mobile networks | Mosh is a reason to buy this kind of app | Standard SSH plus tmux reattachment, which is not Mosh |
| Port forwarding | Local, remote, dynamic SOCKS5 | Local only |
| Host configuration at scale | Synced on iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, Linux; shared host lists | Multiple servers and batch actions (Pro); mobile only |

Read the last three rows first: they are where Agentmux loses.

## Why does Agentmux list tmux sessions first?

Connect to a server and Agentmux lists the tmux sessions already running on it. One tap reattaches, so you do not type `tmux ls` or remember `tmux attach -t`. Reconnect after a drop and you land on the same session, on the screen you left, without retyping anything.

An agent's value is the context it accumulated: which files it read, why it chose this approach. Reattach to that screen and the context survives. Open a fresh prompt and you explain the task again to a process that has forgotten it. What tmux does is the load-bearing part of this design.

## What does the app do while you are away?

Agents routinely run for tens of minutes, and that waiting period is what this is built for. The Dynamic Island and the Lock Screen show progress, and a sound can play when the run ends. The app does not have to sit in the foreground while you stare at it.

An app built around a shell has nothing to report once it is closed, because it holds no notion of a run. Here a named session on a named server is running, and the system reports on it. When that session stops to ask whether to allow a command, AI Permission Review can look first: dangerous commands are held, safe ones get a suggestion or a key press (Pro).

## Can you edit a file without opening vim?

Changing one line of code does not mean wrestling vim on a phone keyboard. The built-in Runestone editor opens the file and lets you edit it. For a README an agent produced, Ink gives a two-column Markdown preview, source and rendered side by side. Git tools (switching branches, reading diffs) and Files app integration are Pro features, available during the 14-day trial.

The loop closes on one device: the agent changes files, you read the diff, you answer, it goes on. Every step that needs a second machine waits for a desk.

## Where do your private keys live?

Private keys go into native secure storage, the iOS Keychain or the Android Keystore, and never into the local database. On iOS, if you turn on iCloud sync, CloudKit carries non-sensitive metadata such as server names. The keys stay where they are.

Ask any tool the same question: which of my private keys leave this device when sync is on? A feature list will not answer it.

## Siri can hand the screen to Shortcuts

`GetCurrentSessionContextIntent` lets you tell Siri "get the current terminal contents from Agentmux". Whatever is on the terminal lands in iOS Shortcuts, ready for Notes, Messages, or anything else you build. `ContinueLastSessionIntent` is blunter: "continue working in Agentmux" reattaches to your last session.

General SSH apps cannot do this, structurally: they have no semantic model of sessions, projects, and agents to expose to the system. Agentmux implements 6 App Intents across four entity types: Server, Project, TMUXSession, RecentSession.

## Fixes you'll feel if you read CJK

Version 1.3.10 fixed three things an English-only user never notices and a Chinese, Japanese, or Korean reader spots at once: selection drifting out of alignment on full-width characters, a link that wraps across lines copying out as several separate pieces, and a lone slash inside CJK text read as a file path.

## Which tool for which job?

**Mostly manual terminal work on one host.** You log in to run commands you chose: restart a service, tail a log, check a disk. Take a general SSH client. If you want to test the idea first, the free single-server tier covers one server, persistent sessions, and the core terminal.

**Living inside agents on several servers.** One refactoring on the Mac mini, another running tests on a Linux box, a third started from a train. That is Agentmux, and specifically Pro: multiple servers, custom agents, remote editing, file history, branch tools, batch actions.

**An agent in a browser tab or a cloud sandbox.** The convenience is real, and the cost is that the files and the credentials no longer sit on your machine. Agentmux never hosts the work: it is a client, and the code and the agent stay on hardware you own, a Mac, a Linux box, or a server. Renting one is defensible if you are at peace with your project and its keys living there.

Tailscale is the recommended way in: no port open to the public internet, and machines addressed by MagicDNS names or 100.x addresses rather than LAN IPs.

## When Termius is the better buy

If one of these is your main job, buy the general tool.

- You work on very unreliable mobile networks and need **Mosh** to hold the connection. Agentmux speaks standard SSH and compensates with automatic tmux reattachment, which is not the same thing as Mosh.

- You need **remote or dynamic (SOCKS5) port forwarding**. Agentmux only does local, and that is a capability gap rather than a preference.

- You want to sync a large host configuration across iOS, Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux, or share a host list with a team. Agentmux is a mobile client: multiple servers and batch actions on Pro, nothing shared.

- You are an SRE or sysadmin running operations across dozens or hundreds of servers. An inventory you script against beats a list you tap through.

Agentmux is built for one workflow: **rejoining a running coding agent from your phone.** It is not a general-purpose operations tool. If your week is a stream of one-off commands, there is nothing here worth switching for.

Decided on Agentmux? The next problem is the machine at the other end: the setup wizard asks three questions and hands back a checklist, and most of what goes wrong afterwards is already in troubleshooting.

## 15 minutes to an agent that works all night

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/setup/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Answer three questions and get the steps for your machine, the agent you want to run, and where you connect from: SSH, tmux, Tailscale.

Setting up an agent that works all night takes about fifteen minutes: SSH into a machine you own, tmux so a dropped phone connection detaches instead of stopping the agent, and Tailscale so no port faces the public internet. Answer three questions about your machine, your agent, and where you connect from, and the wizard builds the checklist.

Every step says why you're doing it, what to run, how to check that it worked, and where to look if it didn't. (Is that machine running Windows? Read this first.)

The setup wizard needs JavaScript. You can also go straight to the troubleshooting page.

## Native Windows has no tmux, so use WSL2

You picked Windows, so the wizard did not hand you a checklist. That path works differently from the other three, and half a checklist would do you more harm than none.

Windows can work, but the route goes through WSL2 and takes a few more steps than a Mac or a Linux box. If all you want is an agent working through the night, rent the cheapest cloud VPS you can find and follow the VPS path above. That is usually faster than getting Windows there, and it saves most people an evening.

### Why won't native Windows do?

This guide rests on three pieces: the CLI, tmux, SSH. SSH is fine. Windows 10 and 11 both ship an OpenSSH Server you can switch on, and you will get a PowerShell prompt.

tmux is the problem. **There is no native Windows build**, and tmux is the load-bearing piece of this whole guide. Without it your phone connection drops, the agent gets SIGHUP, and it dies (the mechanism). "Put your phone away and it keeps running" stops being true. You would have a Windows machine you can SSH into, which is not what this guide is offering.

Whether the agents themselves run on Windows varies by tool and changes quickly, so there is deliberately no list here; check the documentation for the one you plan to use. Mind the order of the argument: **an agent that runs perfectly on native Windows still has no tmux.** Running and surviving a disconnect are separate questions.

### The recommended route: WSL2

Inside WSL2 you have a complete Linux: tmux, sshd, and the agents behave the way they do on real Linux. Install a distribution and every step of the "Linux box" path applies. Go back up and answer the first question that way.

### Three snags that don't exist on Mac or Linux

Knowing them in advance keeps you from assuming you broke something:

- **Networking.** WSL2 runs in a virtual machine with its own IP, behind NAT, so by default nothing outside that Windows host can reach the sshd inside it. There are two ways around it. Forward the port on the Windows side with `netsh interface portproxy`, and expect to redo it, because WSL's IP can change on every restart. Or turn on mirrored networking, `networkingMode=mirrored` in `.wslconfig`, so WSL shares the host's interfaces and the port-forwarding step goes away. Mirrored networking is much cleaner and needs a reasonably recent Windows 11.

- **WSL doesn't stay running on its own.** When the last process exits, the distribution shuts down within seconds and takes the virtual machine with it. You want the machine to stay *always on*, so WSL has to start at boot and keep running with nobody logged in, usually through a scheduled task or a keepalive. There is nothing to do about that on a Mac or a Linux box.

- **systemd is opt-in.** Older WSL has no systemd at all, so `systemctl` does not exist, and the systemd commands in the wizard's "enable the SSH service on the Linux box" step fail outright. Newer versions turn it on with `systemd=true` in `/etc/wsl.conf`, but the default is off.

### What if your Windows PC is the client?

The Windows discussed here is always *the machine you connect to*. If your Windows PC is the computer you work at, and the agent runs somewhere else (a Mac mini at home, a Linux box at the office, a VPS), none of the above applies. The guide works for you as written, and the machine to set up is not the one in front of you.

## Run Claude Code on your iPhone or iPad

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/claude-code-on-iphone/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Claude Code runs on a machine you own, not on the phone. Remote Login, Tailscale, a named tmux session, and the PATH problem SSH causes.

Yes. Claude Code is a program that runs on a machine you own, never on the phone. Turn on Remote Login, reach that machine through Tailscale instead of an open port, start a tmux session with a name, and run `claude` inside it. Your iPhone carries a terminal. The agent keeps working after you lock the screen.

"Claude Code on my phone" names two machines doing two different jobs. Separate them and what is left gets short: what survives a dropped connection, why the command is missing over SSH, and whether an agent should answer its own permission prompts from a train.

## Does Claude Code run on the phone?

Claude Code is a program on the disk of some machine you own. A shell starts it. It reads your project through that machine's filesystem, runs `git` and the tests, and writes its edits back into the same directory. None of that happens in your pocket, though the phrase suggests it does.

From the phone, two things cross the wire: keys go out, characters come back. The agent is not installed there, and no copy of your repository travels. The phone draws a picture of a session running on another computer.

- **On the phone.** Keystrokes, the display, your thumb. Lock the screen or swipe the app away and the display stops, and that is the whole list.

- **On the machine.** The process, the files being edited, the tests, and everything the agent has already read and decided. None of it notices your screen going dark.

Two consequences follow. The machine has to stay on and reachable: a laptop closed in a drawer runs nothing. The phone is the cheap half to replace.

## Three things to set up, in this order

Skip one and the arrangement fails, so work through them in this order.

- **A door into the machine.** On a Mac: System Settings → General → Sharing → **Remote Login**. On Linux, the SSH service, a daemon called `sshd`.

- **A private network instead of an open port.** Install Tailscale on the machine and the phone, sign both into one account, then connect to the MagicDNS name or the `100.x` address. Do not use a LAN address such as `192.168.1.23`, which means nothing on mobile data. Forwarding port 22 instead hands your machine to every scanning bot that finds it.

- **A tmux session with a name, and the agent inside it.**

```
tmux new -s work     # name it
claude               # inside it
```

From the phone, on another network:

```
tmux ls              # what exists
tmux attach -t work  # open a window onto it
```

The name matters: `tmux attach` on its own takes the most recent session, and that is a guess about which one you meant. If tmux is missing, Agentmux installs it.

## Why a plain SSH window kills the agent

Skip tmux: you SSH in, run `claude`, then put the phone in your pocket and lock the screen.

The phone stops sending packets, the connection times out, and it closes. sshd closes the pseudo-terminal that connection was attached to, and the kernel sends **SIGHUP** to every process still attached to it: your shell, and Claude Code running inside your shell. Both take the default reaction and exit, so the agent dies mid-edit with twenty minutes of reading gone.

Keeping the app open fixes nothing. Wi-Fi switches networks, cellular loses signal, one Ctrl-C lands somewhere it should not. tmux moves the session onto the machine itself, so a dropped connection takes the window and leaves the process alone (the mechanism). **The agent goes inside the session before the work starts, because a process that is already running cannot be moved into tmux afterwards.**

## What is working from a phone actually like?

A phone fits one decision at a time, which is what an agent cycle is made of anyway. It proposes a plan, and you take it or send one sentence back. A two-line correction such as "leave the serializer alone, the export job uses it" is enough, and then the phone goes away.

The on-screen keyboard is the first real cost. Backticks, pipes, quotes, backslashes and the tilde all sit two layers deep, so `~/src/auth/session.ts` takes longer than it should, and one wrong segment costs a round trip. Long prompts are harder to proofread than they look, which is why many people draft them in a notes app.

A diff is where a phone runs out of room. Forty changed lines across two files is three screens of scrolling on six inches, and a wrapped line hides whether a change sits at the end of a line or in the middle. Turn an iPad sideways and that same diff fits without wrapping.

One habit pays for itself: a second session for the noisy parts, so a test run cannot bury the agent's prompts.

```
tmux new -s tests -d    # -d starts it detached
tmux attach -t tests    # watch it, then detach
```

## Can the agent answer its own permission prompts?

Claude Code does not run everything it thinks of. Before it runs a command, and depending on your configuration before it edits a file, it stops and asks: here is the command, go ahead? That stop is where the job waits, and if only you can answer it, the waiting becomes the bottleneck.

AI Permission Review answers those prompts and nothing else: it reads the prompt, then suggests or presses the key. A **blacklist** blocks dangerous commands and always hands a match to you. An **allowlist** passes commands you already trust, decided on the device. Anything matching neither goes to an **AI judgement**: allow, deny, or unsure, and the last two come back to you. The session's mode then decides whether it only **suggests** the key or **presses** it.

Distance does not move the responsibility off you. A command you approve on cellular runs on a machine that holds your `.env`, your keys, and a repository you do not own alone, and the judgement sees the screen, not the reasoning that got the agent there. Start in the mode that only suggests, allowlist the commands you approve every day, and read the screen before pressing anything when the signal and your attention are both poor. The blacklist exists because "approve everything" is a bad default: an `rm -rf` aimed at a home directory is no gentler because you said yes on a train platform.

## claude: command not found, but it runs in Terminal

Same machine, same account, two different answers: `claude` starts in Terminal and prints `claude: command not found` over SSH. That reads like the remote setup is broken. It is the most common failure on the way in.

An install through npm, or under a node version nvm pins, writes its directory into a startup file that only an *interactive login* shell reads, and that is how the PATH gets the entry. A connection that runs one command, like `ssh host claude`, starts a non-interactive shell, and that shell never reads the file.

The fix that always works is to stop relying on the PATH. In the Terminal where it runs:

```
which claude
# /Users/you/.nvm/versions/node/v20.11.0/bin/claude
```

Use that absolute path, either as the agent command or typed into the session. It breaks when nvm changes the node version. The durable fix depends on your shell and your distribution, and the troubleshooting page covers it.

## Can the agent work overnight?

A session on a machine that stays awake runs all night: hand it a refactor at eleven and read the result over coffee. Three things get in the way.

**The machine has to stay awake.** A Mac that idles into sleep takes its network interface with it, and Remote Login makes no difference because nothing is left to answer. System Settings → Battery on a laptop, Energy Saver on a desktop: lengthen or switch off idle sleep, and turn on "Wake for network access" if your Mac offers it.

**A reboot takes the session with it.** tmux does not restore sessions after a restart, and a software update reboots the machine without asking. Commit before you stop for the night, so the worst case costs an hour instead of the whole task.

**A session can be waiting rather than dead.** Attach and look. A fresh shell prompt means the process exited: finished, or died, and the lines above say which. A prompt asking you a question has waited six hours for one word, at no cost. From a lock screen both look the same, and only one needs you to act.

## What belongs on the phone, what belongs at the desk

| From the phone | At the desk |
| --- | --- |
| Answer a permission prompt, having read it | Review a diff you did not expect to see |
| Choose between the two approaches it offered | Judge a change spanning several files |
| Read one short diff, commit, push | Read a long diff, or a file you have never opened |
| Watch a test run in a second session | Debug the failure those tests printed |
| Hand it the next task before bed | Write a prompt that has to be exact |
| Reattach after ten dropped connections | Fix the connection, or the PATH problem behind it |

Three things have to hold: a machine that stays awake, a session with a name, and a private way in. If one is missing, the setup wizard asks three questions about your machine and hands back a checklist.

## AI Permission Review: who answers when your agent asks

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/permission-review/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

Who answers when an agent asks to run a command: a local blacklist blocks it, an allowlist clears it, or AI judgement decides.

AI Permission Review answers the permission prompt an agent raises when you are not looking at the screen. A blacklist blocks dangerous commands first, an allowlist passes the commands you already trust, and an AI judgement decides the rest. The session's mode then decides whether it only suggests the key or presses it for you.

Halfway through a task the agent stops and asks "Run this command?" You happen to be away from the screen, and the whole job waits on one key press.

AI Permission Review exists for that moment. It answers the prompt, one key at a time. It does not type the command, and it does not touch anything else on the screen.

- **The agent stops and waits**Agentmux detects a permission prompt

- **Read the screen**Find the current prompt and redact sensitive text

- **Blacklist**A dangerous command matched*Handed to you*

- **Allowlist**A command you trust matched; pick the key locally

- **AI judgement**Allow, deny, or unsure*Deny or unsure: handed to you*

- **Re-check before sending**If the screen changed, nothing is sent*Handed to you*

- **Suggest, or press for you**Depends on the mode you picked

## It starts only when an agent stops and waits

Agentmux already tracks the state of agents like Claude Code and Codex. When a prompt such as "Allow this?" or "Pick 1 or 2" appears on screen, the session is marked as waiting, and the review starts from there.

These also need to be true:

- The AI Permission Review switch in Settings is on.

- The session's mode is Advisor or Auto Reply, not Off.

- You have Pro, or you're still in the free trial.

Each prompt is judged once, and Agentmux does not re-run that check every few seconds. If you press a key or type in the terminal yourself, it cancels the review in progress and takes your input instead.

Switch to another tab and the review keeps running in the background, on the sessions you are no longer looking at.

## It reads the current prompt, not the scrollback

It picks out the prompt currently on screen: the command to run, the question itself, and the choices offered. Anything that has already scrolled up does not count.

Before the screen goes to the AI, Agentmux redacts anything that looks like a password, API key, or token. If that redaction fails, the text is not sent and no key is pressed this time.

## The blacklist runs first, on your phone

Your phone does the matching, and the blacklist runs before anything else. A match is never sent to the AI: the prompt comes straight to you. The built-in rules cover the most dangerous kinds of operations:

- `rm -rf` on `/`, `~`, or your home directory

- `sudo`

- `git push --force` (`--force-with-lease` doesn't count)

- `DROP TABLE`, `DROP DATABASE`, `TRUNCATE TABLE`

- Piping something downloaded straight into a shell, like `curl … | sh`

- Commands that write directly to a disk, like `mkfs` and `dd if=`

You can edit or remove these built-in rules, and add your own.

## The allowlist decides without the AI

Some commands you approve every day, like a test run or a build. Add them to the allowlist and the next match is settled on your phone. It picks the key locally, so there is no wait for the AI and no API usage.

In Auto Reply mode you can also turn on "Allow all commands in this session" for a single session. That skips the AI judgement. The blacklist still applies, and the setting turns itself off when the session ends.

If the allowlist matches but the screen shows no clear, safe key, the prompt comes to you instead.

## What does the AI decide?

Only prompts that match neither list reach the AI. It gets the redacted screen plus your **Main Intent**, which is what you want the agent to do this time, for example "fix the login page tests".

You can choose between two engines:

- **JEV decision engine** (through OpenRouter or TypeSafe): built for terminal prompts, and fast. It decides in three tiers. Safe read-only operations are allowed. Commands that match your Main Intent are allowed. Everything else comes to you, whether it is unrelated, unclear, or high-risk. Anything that looks suspicious or like a malicious injection is denied outright.

- **An OpenAI-compatible LLM**: OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a model you run on your own machine.

The AI reaches one of three conclusions: allow, deny, or unsure. Only "allow" goes further, and the AI has to name the exact option on screen it wants to pick. It never picks a permanent grant such as "Always allow" or "Don't ask again".

## Advisor suggests, Auto Reply presses the key

Each session has its own mode:

- **Advisor** (default): suggestions only. A notice at the top of the screen tells you what it recommends, with an Accept button next to it. Nothing is sent until you tap it.

- **Auto Reply**: when the verdict is allow, it presses the key for you and shows a notice saying which key it pressed.

Either way, it looks at the screen again right before sending a key. If the prompt changed, the options moved, or the cursor is not on the target, it sends nothing. The judgement takes a few seconds, and the prompt can change in that time, so the second look is what stops a wrong option from being pressed.

After Auto Reply sends a key, Agentmux waits 3 seconds before sending another one in that session.

## When does it hand the prompt back to you?

- A blacklist rule matched.

- The AI said deny, or was unsure.

- It cannot tell which key the prompt wants.

- The choice is a permanent grant such as "Always allow".

- The screen changed before the key was sent.

- Redacting the sensitive text failed.

Then Agentmux alerts you the same way it would with the review turned off.

## How do I turn it on?

Before you start, have one of these ready:

- An API key for the JEV engine, from OpenRouter or TypeSafe.

- Your own OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint, such as the OpenAI API or a model running on your own computer.

- Open Settings → AI Permission Review and turn on the switch. The first time, you see an explanation of what data is shared. Tap to agree and it takes you to Advanced Settings.

- In Advanced Settings, choose an engine, enter your API key, and tap "Test AI Endpoint Connection" to confirm that it works.

- Back in Settings, pick a default under Permission Review Mode (Advisor is a reasonable start), then write your Main Intent.

- Connect to a server and start an agent. New tabs start in the default mode. To change the mode or the Main Intent for one session, tap the Permission Review button in the terminal toolbar. There you can also turn on "Use My Latest Prompt", so the Main Intent follows each prompt you send in that tab.

Run Advisor for a few days first and compare its suggestions with how you actually answer. Then turn on Auto Reply for the sessions where the pattern holds.

## What data leaves your device?

Only two things leave it: the redacted text on screen and your Main Intent. They go to the AI service you set up, using your own API key. With "Use My Latest Prompt" on, the prompts you send in that tab become the Main Intent, so they are sent as well. Agentmux does not provide or relay an AI service. The record of each decision stays on your device, where you can review or clear it in the audit log. Model reasoning is not stored.

## Stuck? Start here

URL: https://agentmux.saxcave.cc/guide/en/troubleshooting/
Language: en
Updated: 2026-11-06

SSH refused, key rejected, tmux missing, claude not found: eight failures, each with a cause and a command to type.

Remote development over SSH, tmux and Tailscale fails in eight recognizable ways: `Operation timed out`, `Permission denied (publickey)`, a password that is correct but rejected, `tmux not found`, `claude: command not found`, Tailscale showing connected but unreachable, Remote Login on but the Mac refusing, and `sudo: a terminal is required`. Each one has a symptom, a cause, and a fix.

Follow the previous articles and it works first time eight or nine times out of ten. When it does not, it is almost always one of these eight. Find your error message and jump to it. Nobody needs to read this page from the top.

## Connection timed out (Operation timed out)

### Symptom

You run `ssh user@host` and the screen just sits there. After a long wait comes `Operation timed out` or `Connection timed out`. SSH never gets as far as asking you for a password.

### Causes

- A typo in the hostname, say `my-serverr`. SSH reports `Could not resolve hostname` straight away instead of hanging, so if you see that message, go check the spelling. A hang means a wrong IP: a missing octet, one wrong digit, or an address where nothing is listening.

- SSH isn't on the standard port 22 on the other end and you left out `-p`.

- The target machine is asleep, or simply switched off.

- A firewall in between is dropping the connection: your home router, a corporate network, hotel Wi-Fi. The machine never receives your request.

### Fix

A timeout means your packets never reached the machine, so confirm one hop at a time instead of guessing. First check whether the machine responds at all:

```
ping host-address
```

Nothing back from `ping`? Check the IP for typos, then check whether the machine is asleep or powered off. Some machines block `ping` on purpose, so a failure here does not prove the machine is unreachable. Go straight to the next step.

Next, check whether anything is actually listening on the SSH port:

```
nc -vzw 5 host-address 22
```

Replace `22` with the port the other end really uses. The `-w 5` caps the wait at five seconds, so a blocked port gives you an answer instead of hanging.

You get one of three outcomes. `succeeded` or `open`: the port is reachable, so the problem is elsewhere. `Connection refused`: the machine received you, but nothing is listening there. Another timeout: something in between is dropping the packets, usually a firewall. Look at the router configuration or the network you are on, not at the server.

## Permission denied (publickey)

### Symptom

The connection is refused the instant you make it. It prints `Permission denied (publickey).` and never asks you for a password.

### Cause

The server will not accept the key you are presenting. Most often the public key was never put on the server at all.

The other cause is easy to miss: permissions on `~/.ssh` or `authorized_keys` that are too loose. SSH is strict here. If the permissions are wrong it ignores the file completely, no matter how correct the key inside is.

### Fix

When a key is refused, the usual reason is that the server never received it. If you have not copied the public key across, the quickest route is `ssh-copy-id`: it logs in once with a password and appends your local public key to the server's `authorized_keys`.

```
ssh-copy-id user@host
```

That assumes password login is still enabled on the server. If it has already been turned off (see Password is correct but rejected below), you'll need someone with console access to that machine to paste the public key into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` directly.

If the key really is in there, one per line, complete and not truncated, and you are still refused, permissions are the likely culprit. Check them against the table. The last row is the one people miss: get `~/.ssh` and `authorized_keys` both right, leave your home directory group- or world-writable, and `StrictModes` still refuses.

| Path | Required permissions | Command |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~/.ssh | 700 | chmod 700 ~/.ssh |
| ~/.ssh/authorized_keys | 600 | chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys |
| ~ (the home directory itself) | Not writable by group or others | chmod go-w ~ |

Try connecting again once the permissions are fixed. If it still fails, add `-v` locally to watch the exchange and confirm SSH is really offering the key you think it is:

```
ssh -v user@host
```

That runs to fifty or sixty lines. You only need two of them. `Offering public key: ...` means your key really was sent, so nothing is wrong at your end. If `Authentications that can continue: publickey` follows it, the server received the key and declined it. The key is in the wrong place or the permissions are wrong, so carry on with the steps above.

## Password is correct but rejected

### Symptom

You're certain the password is right, and you may well have pasted it, but SSH keeps returning `Permission denied, please try again.` Sometimes it ends without prompting you at all.

### Cause

This usually has nothing to do with the password. The server's SSH configuration has password authentication switched off (`PasswordAuthentication no`). That is a common hardening choice: it forces everyone onto keys and removes password guessing as an attack. With it set, a correct password gets refused a hundred times out of a hundred.

The next part costs people more time than anything else on this page. Newer systems (Ubuntu after 22.10, Debian 12, nearly every cloud provider's default image) put a line near the top of `sshd_config` reading `Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf`, which pulls in every config file in that directory. For any one setting, sshd keeps the *first* value it reads, so a later one does not override it.

If `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` holds something like `50-cloud-init.conf` that also says `PasswordAuthentication no`, that file wins over the line you just edited in the main file. You save the file, restart the service, and you are still refused.

### Fix

The better fix is key authentication: see Permission denied (publickey) above for getting your public key into the server's `authorized_keys`.

Only change the configuration if you administer this server and have decided you do want password login. First find out whether another file will override the value you're about to edit:

```
sudo grep -r PasswordAuthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
```

If a file under `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` also sets `PasswordAuthentication`, change that value too (or comment the line out). Once that's clean, edit `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` and set `PasswordAuthentication` to `yes`.

**Don't close your current connection yet.** A broken sshd configuration can lock you out of the machine for good. Keep this window as your way back in until the new one is confirmed working. Check the syntax before anything else:

```
sudo sshd -t
```

When it prints no errors, restart the service to apply the change:

```
sudo systemctl restart ssh
```

On some distributions the service is called `sshd` rather than `ssh`. If the line above cannot find it, try `sudo systemctl restart sshd`. Then open a brand-new connection, not the one you kept as a fallback, and confirm password login works. Close the old window only after that.
